summary: Most visitors to Chad need a visa arranged in advance through a Chadian embassy — an electronic visa has been announced but the rollout is still patchy — while citizens of fellow CEMAC states enter visa-free. Border regions carry serious security risks.

notes: Photography requires care. A permit has historically been required, and photographing military sites, airports and official buildings is prohibited.
Export of animal products and cultural artefacts without authorization is prohibited.

payments.text: Cash rules. Cards are accepted only at one or two international hotels in N'Djamena and ATMs are scarce and unreliable. Bring CFA francs or euros to exchange, and carry enough cash for any travel outside the capital.

safety.text: Governments advise against travel to Chad's border zones — the Lake Chad basin (Boko Haram activity) and the borders with Libya, Sudan and the Central African Republic — and against all nonessential travel to much of the rest of the country. N'Djamena is calmer but armed banditry and sudden unrest remain risks.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Chad Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: November to February brings the coolest, driest conditions — the season for Zakouma National Park and expeditions to the Ennedi massif; from March the heat becomes extreme, and the July–September rains close many routes.

tips.text: Stay away from the Lake Chad basin and the borders with Libya, Sudan and the Central African Republic — these areas see jihadist activity, armed banditry and military operations, and most governments classify them as no-go zones.

Chad has announced an electronic visa, but the rollout has been uneven — do not rely on it. Until you have confirmation from a Chadian embassy that the eVisa works for your nationality and entry point, apply for a standard embassy visa.
Register with the immigration authorities (Sûreté Nationale) within 72 hours of arrival — hotels in N'Djamena can usually help, and the stamp is checked when you leave.
Be extremely careful with cameras — photographing airports, bridges, government buildings or anything military can lead to arrest, and a general photography permit has historically been required.
Zakouma National Park — one of Africa's great conservation revivals — is Chad's standout draw; visits run November to April and are best booked through the park's official operators well in advance.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Chad?
faq.answer: Yes, unless you hold a passport from a CEMAC state (Cameroon, Central African Republic, Congo, Gabon or Equatorial Guinea). Everyone else should obtain a visa from a Chadian embassy before travel.

faq.question: Does Chad have an eVisa?
faq.answer: Chad has announced an electronic visa, but availability has been inconsistent since launch. Confirm with the nearest Chadian embassy whether the eVisa currently works for your nationality, and if in doubt, apply for a standard embassy visa.

faq.question: Is Chad safe for tourists?
faq.answer: Only partly. N'Djamena, Zakouma National Park and organized Ennedi expeditions see travelers without incident, but the Lake Chad basin and the borders with Libya, Sudan and the Central African Republic are no-go zones. Check current government travel advice before booking.

faq.question: Do I have to register after arriving in Chad?
faq.answer: Yes — foreign visitors are expected to register with the immigration authorities within about 72 hours of arrival. Hotels in N'Djamena can usually arrange it; keep the receipt, as it may be checked on departure.

faq.question: Do I need a yellow fever vaccination for Chad?
faq.answer: A certificate is formally required if you arrive from a country with yellow fever risk, and vaccination is strongly recommended for all travelers — in practice officials often ask for the yellow card regardless of where you flew from.
